Explanation

Your application has hardcoded URLs that might correspond to services that are not accessible on Azure.

Review and ensure that the application is attempting to access URLs that would be available from Azure. You might need to migrate those services to Azure too, this way you will get the benefit of lower latency in the cloud.

If your application needs to depend on services that run on-premises, you can connect your Azure and local networks with ExpressRoute, Hybrid Connections, or VPN solutions.
SQL database connection detected
 Potential 3
FilePosition
src\eShopWCFService\Web.config

Explanation

SQL database connection detected.

Ensure the database is available/reachable on Azure.

If it is not, there are multiple ways you can move your data to Azure:
1. Migrate to Azure SQL Database.
2. Consider Azure SQL Managed Instance if you need features that are not available in Azure SQL Database and you don’t want to use a VM.
3. Migrate your database servers directly to SQL Server on Azure VMs.

To assess database migration effort, you can use Azure Migrate tool, see the link below.
Local or network IO operations detected
 Potential 3
FilePosition
src\eShopWinForms\Views\CatalogView.csLine 57

Explanation

Your application has local or network IO operations.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, move persistent I/O to storage mounts (Azure Files/UNC). Keep local writes to temp only; connect to external dependencies via private endpoints/VNet to reduce latency.

IO operations outside of the application folder might not be available on Azure App Service. Review and ensure IO APIs are attempting to access paths that will be available when your app is running on App Service sandbox. If you choose the containerized hosting option, your scenario still might be broken or have scalability issues.

Possible solutions:
1. Files that the application needs can be deployed with the application or put in Azure Storage. You can use Azure Storage File Shares as a drop-in replacement for on-premises file share.
2. Other services that the application depends on might need to be migrated to Azure, this way you will get the benefit of lower latency in the cloud.
3. If your application needs to depend on services that run on-premise, you can connect your Azure and local networks with ExpressRoute, Hybrid Connections, or VPN solutions.
Local OS environment access detected
 Potential 1
FilePosition
src\eShopWinForms\Views\CatalogView.csLine 56

Explanation

Local OS environment access detected.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, Read config via App Settings or App Configuration; avoid machine‑specific environment APIs. Persist environment setup via install scripts when needed.

When running in Azure App Service environment, your application can read environment variables that you define in App Service settings. Using environment API other than reading environment variables might indicate that your application depends on some local machine's features and might be broken on App Service sandbox or not scale well. Review your scenarios and either refactor them to be more cloud friendly or choose the option in App Service to host your application in the sandbox for Windows Container Web Apps.

If you choose to use other Azure hosting options such as Azure Container Apps (ACA) or Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), environment APIs might work, however scaling still might be an issue.
Upgrade to newer target framework to get better cloud experience
 Optional 3
FilePosition
src\eShopWCFService\eShopWCFService.csproj
src\eShopWinForms\eShopWinForms.csproj

Explanation

Upgrade to newer target framework to get better cloud experience.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, validate on .NET Framework 4.8 or move to .NET 10. Persist any runtime prerequisites via install scripts; test in staging before production.

While if targeting other Azure compute services:

Application targeting .NET framework lower than 4.7.1 might missing features that would be needed for some cloud scenarios like scaling or getting secrets from secure external sources.

Azure App Service runs apps on .NET Framework 4.8 or .NET Framework 3.5. Apps running on on .NET Framework versions older than .NET Framework 4.8 could have potential compatibility issues. It is recommended to test your application running on .NET Framework 4.8. Note that it is not necessary to re-target to .NET Framework 4.8, only to validate that the app correctly runs on that version of .NET Framework.

In the long term it is also recommended to upgrade your application to latest supported .NET 8+ which would significantly increase performance of your application. Use tools like .NET Upgrade Assistant to help with upgrading your application to newer .NET.
Connection strings without configuration builders detected
 Optional 3
FilePosition
src\eShopWCFService\Web.config
src\eShopWCFService\Web.config

Explanation

Connection strings without configuration builders detected.

Keeping connection strings directly in the app is not the best practice and might introduce security risks, increased maintenance, scalability challenges or compliance standards (such as PCI DSS, GDPR, etc.).

Instead, it is recommended to use configuration builders to get secrets from secure sources in Azure environment.
System.Data.SqlClient dependency detected
 Optional 3
FilePosition
src\eShopWCFService\Web.config

Explanation

System.Data.SqlClient dependency is detected.

While System.Data.SqlClient will work in Azure, the newer Microsoft.Data.SqlClient package is the primary .NET SQL client moving forward and receiving the latest features. For example, Microsoft.Data.SqlClient easily allows use of Azure Managed Identity from a connection string.

Explanation

Static content detected.

Your current approach of serving static content directly might lead to increased costs, performance issues, maintenance challenges (requiring application redeployment for content changes), and security risks.

Consider moving static content to Azure Blob Storage and adding Azure CDN.

WCF Client APIs
 Mandatory 1
FilePosition

Explanation

WCF client-side APIs for building service clients that communicate with WCF services. These APIs are available as exact equivalents via NuGet packages - add System.ServiceModel.* NuGet packages (System.ServiceModel.Http, System.ServiceModel.Primitives, System.ServiceModel.NetTcp, etc.)
Legacy Configuration System
 Mandatory 2
FilePosition

Explanation

Legacy XML-based configuration system (app.config/web.config) that has been replaced by a more flexible configuration model in .NET Core. The old system was rigid and XML-based. Migrate to Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration with JSON/environment variables; use System.Configuration.ConfigurationManager NuGet package as interim bridge if needed.
GDI+ / System.Drawing
 Mandatory 1
FilePosition

Explanation

System.Drawing APIs for 2D graphics, imaging, and printing that are available via NuGet package System.Drawing.Common. Note: Not recommended for server scenarios due to Windows dependencies; consider cross-platform alternatives like SkiaSharp or ImageSharp for new code.
Windows Forms Legacy Controls
 Mandatory 3
FilePosition

Explanation

Legacy Windows Forms controls that have been removed from .NET Core/5+ including StatusBar, DataGrid, ContextMenu, MainMenu, MenuItem, and ToolBar. These controls were replaced by more modern alternatives. Use ToolStrip, MenuStrip, ContextMenuStrip, and DataGridView instead.
Windows Forms
 Mandatory 1
FilePosition

Explanation

Windows Forms APIs for building Windows desktop applications with traditional Forms-based UI that are available in .NET on Windows. Enable Windows Desktop support: Option 1 (Recommended): Target net9.0-windows; Option 2: Add <UseWindowsDesktop>true</UseWindowsDesktop>; Option 3 (Legacy): Use Microsoft.NET.Sdk.WindowsDesktop SDK.

Data Storage & External Services

The WCF service uses one SQL Server LocalDB database (eShopDatabase) through Entity Framework. The desktop client calls the service at a configured local HTTP endpoint; no other external APIs, caches, or message brokers were found.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • The solution separates the desktop UI from persistence behind the ICatalogService WCF contract.
  • CatalogController mediates view events and synchronous service calls.
  • EntityModel is the EF6 DbContext; service methods query its sets directly. A mock service implementation exists but is not wired into the application startup.

DTOs & Contracts

The WCF contract uses mutable [DataContract] model classes: CatalogItem, CatalogBrand, CatalogType, CatalogItemsStock, and DiscountItem. They are service-level domain entities and request/response DTOs; no immutable record types, OpenAPI/Swagger specification, protobuf schema, or GraphQL schema was found. WCF uses its data-contract serialization; Newtonsoft.Json is used in the client helper for local JSON data rather than this SOAP contract.

Communication Patterns

Communication is synchronous WCF SOAP using basicHttpBinding at the local client endpoint. The service uses direct method calls and EF6; there is no message broker, service discovery, API gateway, client-side load balancing, retry policy, circuit breaker, or configured timeout policy in the inspected project files.

No application-level authentication or authorization configuration was identified for the WCF operations. The WinForms endpoint is HTTP, and the service explicitly declares a basicHttpBinding endpoint; the HTTPS protocol mapping does not change that explicit binding. Host-level IIS policy is outside the available project configuration.

Core Business Workflows

The application supports product catalog browsing and basic inventory availability management for an eShop operator. Users view product details and discounts, search stock by product and date, and record incoming stock.

Domain Entities

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships
CatalogItemCatalogA product offered in the catalogBelongs to a brand and type; has inventory records
CatalogBrandCatalogBrand classification for productsGroups catalog items
CatalogTypeCatalogProduct type classificationGroups catalog items
CatalogItemsStockInventoryAvailable quantity recorded for an item and dateRefers to a catalog item by identifier
DiscountItemPricingDiscount active during a date intervalApplies to displayed catalog prices

Service-to-Domain Mapping

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
eShopWinFormsCatalog and inventory user interfaceNone; consumes service DTOsCatalogService.svc
eShopWCFServiceCatalog, pricing, and inventoryCatalogItem, CatalogBrand, CatalogType, CatalogItemsStock, DiscountItemEntity Framework and SQL Server LocalDB

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Browse and filter the catalog

At startup the CatalogController requests the current discount, catalog items, brand filters, and type filters. Selecting a brand or type raises a view event, and the controller calls GetCatalogItems with the selected identifiers. A filter value of zero represents “all”; the service returns matching items for the view to display.

Workflow 2: Check and record stock availability

The user selects a product and date to query GetAvailableStock. To record incoming inventory, the view parses the selected product, quantity, and arrival date and raises an event. The controller sends a CatalogItemsStock object to CreateAvailableStock; the service updates an existing item/date record or creates a new stock record, then the UI confirms the operation.

Workflow 3: Apply an active discount

The controller requests the discount for the current date. The service returns a discount whose start and end dates contain the requested date; the client applies the returned discount value to displayed prices and updates the banner.

Cross-Service Data Flows

The desktop client calls the WCF service for catalog and stock data. The WCF service reads or updates its EF6 context, which persists to the LocalDB database. No multi-service aggregation, asynchronous event flow, or fallback service is configured. The in-memory mock service exists in source but no activation path was found in application startup.

Business Workflow Sequence

sequenceDiagram participant User participant View as "CatalogView" participant Controller as "CatalogController" participant Client as "WCF Client" participant Service as "CatalogService" participant DB as "SQL Server LocalDB" User->>View: Select item and arrival date View->>View: Check required UI values and parse quantity/date View->>Controller: Raise availability event Controller->>Client: CreateAvailableStock(stock record) Client->>Service: SOAP request Service->>DB: Find stock by product and date alt Stock record exists DB-->>Service: Existing stock Service->>DB: Update available quantity else Stock record does not exist DB-->>Service: No matching stock record Service->>DB: Insert stock record with next identifier end DB-->>Service: Save completed Service-->>Client: Operation completed Client-->>Controller: Return Controller-->>View: Notify availability updated View-->>User: Show confirmation and clear entry fields

Business Rules & Decision Logic

  • Brand and type filter identifier 0 means no filter.
  • A discount is eligible when the requested date is on or after its start date and on or before its end date.
  • Stock is looked up by catalog item identifier and date; a matching record is updated, otherwise a new record is created.
  • New catalog and stock identifiers are derived from the current maximum identifier plus one.
  • The view rejects empty stock fields and parses quantity and date before submitting; no service-side validation or business authorization was identified.
  • EF SaveChanges persists service mutations. No explicit transaction orchestration, audit trail, or compensating workflow was found.

Version & Compatibility Risks

Both projects use legacy non-SDK project files and target .NET Framework 4.7 or 4.6.1. The declared Newtonsoft.Json 6.0.4 dependency is affected by CVE-2024-21907; GitHub lists 13.0.1 as the first patched version. Entity Framework 6.1.3 and Web API Client 5.2.3 are also old package versions that require compatibility review for modernization.

Notable Observations

  • Entity Framework is declared in both the client and service projects, although database operations are implemented in the service.
  • The WinForms app uses a generated WCF client and .NET Framework service assemblies rather than a separately declared modern HTTP client.
  • No package lock file or centralized package management file was found, so resolved transitive versions are not pinned in repository metadata.

erDiagram CatalogBrand ||--o{ CatalogItem : "brands" CatalogType ||--o{ CatalogItem : "categorizes" CatalogItem ||--o{ CatalogItemsStock : "stock entries by item id" CatalogBrand { int Id PK string Brand } CatalogType { int Id PK string Type } CatalogItem { int Id PK string Name decimal Price int CatalogBrandId FK int CatalogTypeId FK } CatalogItemsStock { int StockId PK int CatalogItemId date Date int AvailableStock } DiscountItem { int Id PK date Start date End float Size }

CatalogItem references its brand and type through EF-convention foreign keys. Caching Strategy

No application-level cache provider or cache annotations were detected. The desktop view keeps displayed results in its UI controls; no server-side cache strategy is configured.

The WCF service is the single owner of one shared LocalDB database. The WinForms client does not access the database directly; it requests catalog, discount, and stock data through ICatalogService. There are no separate service databases, cross-service joins, CQRS projections, or messaging-based data flows.
